case_prompt: A 29-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with epigastric abdominal pain. He reported a 1-week history of tea-colored urine, pale stools, and diffuse pruritus that preceded the development of a new rash. He denied taking any medications, including over-the-counter herbal supplements or analgesics. He drank alcohol occasionally (2–3 standard drinks several days per month). He identified as a man who has sex with men and reported unprotected sexual encounters with multiple partners several months before symptom onset. On examination, he had a diffuse papular rash involving the palms, soles, trunk, face, and groin, as well as scleral icterus; the abdomen was soft, without hepatomegaly or tenderness. Laboratory studies showed an alkaline phosphatase level of 279 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L, alanine transaminase 167 U/L, total bilirubin 5.6 mg/dL (conjugated bilirubin 3.7 mg/dL), and serum albumin 2.6 g/dL. Urinalysis revealed 3+ bilirubin and 4+ protein; serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL. The random urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 6,667 mg/g, and a 24-hour urine collection showed 13.3 g of protein. Five days before presentation, antimitochondrial antibody and antismooth muscle antibody had returned positive (AMA 57 U; ASMA 31 U). Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were negative. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated moderate intrahepatic biliary dilation and heterogeneous perfusion of the liver. Hepatology was consulted and recommended evaluation for systemic infectious or inflammatory etiologies and repeat autoantibody testing.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Medication-induced cholestasis was considered but excluded based on history — “He denied taking any medications including over-the-counter herbal supplements or analgesics.” 2. Acute viral hepatitis was considered but excluded after testing — “Hepatitis screen was negative for acute hepatitis A, B, or C infection.” 3. Primary biliary cholangitis was considered given cholestatic injury and positive AMA but excluded because “In this case, the patient presented with features atypical of PBC, such as a diffuse rash along the palms and soles, biliary dilatation, evidence of glomerular injury, and a sudden onset of symptoms.” 4. Secondary syphilis was suspected based on rash and sexual risk factors — “Considering the patient's rash, the history of unprotected sex, and high-risk group (MSM), syphilis screening was performed.”

selection.screen_reason: Sexual history, palm-and-sole rash, cholestatic hepatitis and nephrotic proteinuria make secondary syphilis reachable, with serology as the orderable confirmation.
selection.second_look_note: Unprotected sex with multiple male partners, a palm-and-sole rash, cholestatic hepatitis and nephrotic proteinuria; the sexual history is the key clue to secondary syphilis.
